accepted.question_text: Can one identify abstract classes of variational objectives on probability measures and corresponding random approximations such that the objective values E(mu_n) converge to E(mu_*) as the number of samples grows, quantitative convergence rates can be proved under explicit model assumptions, and the resulting abstract classes still cover problems of practical interest in machine learning?

evidence.quote: Our vision leads to the following theoretical problem: Can we define abstract classes of objectives E and of their (random) approximations En , such that E(µn ) converges to E(µ∗ ) as n goes to infinity? Can we give rates of convergence of such a convergence under some well-specified model assumptions? Do those abstract classes describe problems of practical interest?

accepted.question_text: Can one define practical variational objectives on measures and corresponding random approximations such that minimizing the approximation E_n produces a distribution mu_n with favorable practical properties, and can one exhibit concrete machine-learning applications in which this measure-based perspective advances the state of the art?

evidence.quote: Those questions could equally be explored from the practical side. Can we define objectives E and of their (random) approximations En , such that trying to minimize En leads to distribution µn with favorable practical properties? Can we find examples where this perspective advances the state-of-the art of a machine learning application?
